# 1 Samuel Chapter 21 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 163v–164r | **Source Images:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/1SA_021_page_001.jpg, 1SA_021_page_002.jpg

---

**1** David went to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech came trembling to meet him and asked, "Why are you alone? Why is no one with you?"

**2** David told the priest, "The king has sent me on a mission and instructed me: 'No one is to know anything about the mission I am sending you on or what I have ordered you to do.' As for my men, I have arranged to meet them at a certain place. **3** Now then, what do you have on hand? Give me five loaves of bread, or whatever you can find."

**4** The priest answered David, "I have no ordinary bread on hand — only consecrated bread. The men may have it if they have kept themselves from women." **5** David replied, "Indeed, women have been kept from us as always when I set out on a campaign. The men's bodies are ritually clean even on ordinary missions — how much more so today!" **6** So the priest gave him the consecrated bread, since there was no other bread there except the bread of the Presence that had been removed from before the LORD and replaced with warm bread on the day it was taken away.

**7** Now one of Saul's servants happened to be there that day, detained before the LORD. His name was Doeg the Edomite, chief of Saul's shepherds.

**8** David asked Ahimelech, "Don't you have a spear or a sword here? I didn't bring my sword or any other weapon, because the king's mission was urgent." **9** The priest said, "The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you struck down in the Valley of Elah — it is here, wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you want to take it, take it. There is no other sword here except that one." David said, "There is none like it. Give it to me."

**10** That day David fled from Saul and went to Achish king of Gath. **11** But the servants of Achish said to him, "Isn't this David, the king of the land? Isn't this the one they sing about in their dances: 'Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands'?"

**12** David took these words to heart and became very afraid of Achish king of Gath. **13** So he changed his behavior in their presence and pretended to be insane while in their custody. He scratched marks on the doors of the gate and let his saliva run down his beard.

**14** Achish said to his servants, "Look at the man — he's out of his mind! Why bring him to me? **15** Do I lack madmen that you have brought this one to carry on like a lunatic in my presence? Should this fellow come into my house?"

**16** David left there and escaped to the cave of Adullam. When his brothers and his father's entire household heard about it, they went down to him there.

---

## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

The Hebrew numbering of this chapter differs from English versions; in the Leningrad Codex, the chapter begins at what English Bibles often label as 20:42b or 21:1, with David's departure from Jonathan. I have followed the Hebrew verse numbering throughout, yielding 16 verses.

The phrase *lechem haPanim* (v. 6, "bread of the Presence") refers to the twelve loaves placed weekly before the LORD in the tabernacle — holy bread normally reserved for priests alone. David's appeal and Ahimelech's concession become a landmark case in biblical ethics: Jesus himself cites this episode (Mark 2:25-26) to establish that human need can take precedence over ritual regulation.

David's feigned madness before Achish (*vayeshanno et ta'mo*, literally "he changed his discernment") involves a deliberate performance of insanity. The verb *vayithollel* carries overtones of prophetic frenzy — the same root used for ecstatic behavior. The irony is bitter: the anointed future king of Israel must degrade himself to survive, scratching at gates like a wild animal.

Doeg the Edomite appears here as a seemingly minor detail — "detained before the LORD" — yet his presence at the sanctuary is the fuse that will ignite the massacre of the priests in the next chapter. The narrator plants this detail with devastating economy.

— PNEUMA
